Use context to determine the meaning of a word or phrase.
Use common, grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots to determine the meaning of a word (e.g., audience, auditory, audible, etc.).
Consult reference materials, both print and digital, to find the pronunciation of a word or determine or clarify its precise meaning or its part of speech.
Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase.
Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
Interpret figures of speech (e.g., personification) in context.
Use the relationship between particular words (e.g., cause/effect, part/whole, item/category) to better understand each word.
Distinguish among the connotations (associations) of words with similar denotations (definitions) (e.g., stingy, scrimping, economical, unwasteful, thrifty).
Acquire and use grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.
Gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.
Apply knowledge of vocabulary to reading, writing, speaking, and listening.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
Introduce claim(s) and organize the reasons and evidence clearly.
Support claim(s) with clear reasons and relevant evidence, using credible sources and demonstrating an understanding of the topic or text.
Use varied syntax, words, phrases, and clauses, to clarify the relationships among claim(s) and reasons.
Establish and maintain a formal style.
Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from the argument presented.
Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.

Introduce a topic; organize ideas, concepts, and information, using strategies such as definition, classification, comparison/contrast, and cause/effect; include formatting (e.g., headings, etc.), graphics (e.g., charts, tables, etc.), and multimedia when useful to aid comprehension.
Develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples.
Use appropriate transitions to clarify the relationships among ideas and concepts.
Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
Establish and maintain a formal style.
Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from the information or explanation presented.

Write narratives and other creative texts (e.g. poetry, graphic stories, digital compositions, memoirs) to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, relevant descriptive details, and well-structured event sequences.
Engage and orient the reader by establishing a context and introducing a narrator and/or characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally and logically.
Use literary and narrative techniques, such as dialogue, pacing, rhythm, description, and poetic devices to develop experiences, events, and/or characters.
Use a variety of transition words, phrases, and clauses to convey sequence and signal shifts from one time frame or setting to another.
Use precise words and phrases, relevant descriptive details, figurative and sensory language to convey experiences and events.
Provide a conclusion that follows from and/or reflects the narrated experiences or event (when appropriate to the genre).

Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, style, tone, and voice are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience. (Grade-specific expectations for writing types are defined in standards 1–3 above.)
Develop and strengthen writing as needed.
Employ the writing process by planning, drafting, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.
Use guidance and support from peers, adults, and digital tools. (Editing for conventions should demonstrate command of Language standards 1–3 up to and including grade 6.).
Use technology, including digital tools/platforms, to produce and publish writing.
Link to and cite sources with a standard format such as MLA or APA.
Demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to produce writing with a minimum of two-three pages in a single sitting.
Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and refocusing the inquiry when appropriate.
ather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources.
Assess the credibility of each source.
Quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and providing basic bibliographic information for sources.

Draw relevant evidence from literary or informational texts to support written analysis, reflection, and research, applying one or more grade 6 standards for Reading Literature or Reading Informational texts.

Write routinely over extended time frames (for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences; independently select writing topics and formats for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks.

Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with partners on grade 6 topics, texts, and issues, building on others’ ideas and expressing their own clearly.

Come to discussions prepared having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to respond, probe, and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Follow norms for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.
Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.
Cooperate, mediate, and problem solve to make decisions as appropriate for productive group discussion.
Interpret information presented in diverse media and formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively, orally) and explain how it contributes to a topic, text, or issue under study.
Delineate a speaker’s argument and specific claims, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
Present claims and findings appropriate to the purpose and audience.
Use pertinent descriptions, facts, and details to accentuate main ideas or themes.
Use appropriate vocabulary, eye contact, adequate volume, and clear pronunciation.
Include relevant multimedia components and visual displays in presentations to clarify information.

Adapt speech to a variety of contexts, audience, and tasks, using feedback from self and others and demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate. (See grade 6 Language standards 1 and 3 for specific expectations.)

sets.subject: Mathematics (2026-)
sets.title: 3rd Grade
sets.doc: South Dakota Mathematic Standards
standards: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.
Compose and decompose four-digit numbers into thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones.
Read and write whole numbers up to 10,000 using standard form, word form, and expanded form.
Use visual models (e.g., arrays, equal groups, number lines) to explain and justify multiplication as combining equal groups.
Use visual models (e.g., arrays, equal groups, number lines) to explain and justify division as separating into equal groups.
Solve word problems using multiplication and division within 100 using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown quantities.
Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating to three whole numbers.
Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.
Understand that multiplication and division are inverse operations.
Demonstrate understanding of multiplication and division within 100 by using arrays, equal groups, and number lines to explain the relationship between the two operations.
Demonstrate understanding of addition and multiplication problems using properties (commutative, associative, and identity).

Solve two-step word problems using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division using an equation with a symbol for the unknown quantity; Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
Understand the denominator of a fraction represents the number of equal parts the whole is broken into.
Understand the numerator of a fraction represents the number of selected equal parts.
Understand fractions as parts of a whole, as numbers on a number line, and as multiples of unit fractions.
Use number lines and area models to explain why two fractions are equivalent and how they represent the same quantity (include fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8).
Recognize and generate equivalent fractions and explain why they are equivalent.
Express whole number fractions and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.
Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator using the symbols , =.
Understand area to be the amount of space inside a two-dimensional shape.
Understand a square unit to be a square that is 1 unit on each side and is used to measure area.
Understand a shape has an area of 𝑛𝑛 square units if it can be covered with 𝑛𝑛 unit squares without gaps or overlaps.
Use tiling and visual models to explain how multiplying side lengths of a rectangle represents its area.
Solve word problems involving areas of rectangles.
Use tiling with area models to represent the distributive property of multiplication.
Understand that area can be found by adding the areas of non-overlapping rectangles and use this method to solve real-world problems.
Understand perimeter as the distance around a two-dimensional shape.

Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding unknown side lengths, and creating rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.
Measure and estimate liquid volumes using the U.S. Customary and metric system.
Measure and estimate masses of objects using the U.S. Customary and metric system.
Solve one-step addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division word problems involving masses or volumes in the same units.
Measure lengths using rulers to halves and fourths of an inch.
Tell and write time to the nearest minute using an analog and digital clock.
When solving word problems add, subtract, multiply and divide time to the minute.
Determine the value of a collection of U.S. coins and bills up to $100.00 using decimal notation.
Create a scaled table, bar graph, circle graph, and line graph to represent a given set of data.
Interpret and analyze one and two -step data problems with scaled tables, bar graphs, circle graphs, and line graphs.
Make a line plot using horizontal scale marked off in whole numbers, halves, or quarters.
Understand that shapes in different categories may share attributes and can define a larger category.
Understand that a quadrilateral is any four-sided shape, and identify and describe the relationships between various quadrilaterals, including trapezoids, parallelograms, rectangles, and squares.
Break apart shapes into parts with equal areas and express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
Determine whether a shape is a polygon or non-polygon.
Classify polygons based on the number of sides.
Fluently use multiplication strategies to mentally solve multiplication facts through 12.
Recall from memory multiplication facts (0-12) to include 0, 1, 2, 5, and 10.
Fluently add within 1,000 using various strategies.
Fluently subtract within 1,000 using various strategies.
Fluently multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10-90.

sets.subject: Mathematics (2026-)
sets.title: 2nd Grade
sets.doc: South Dakota Mathematic Standards
standards: Count forward and backward from any number by 10s and 100s up to 1000.
Count forward and backward by 5s to 120.
Count forward and backward by 2s to 50
Determine whether a number is odd or even within 50.
Given a two-digit or three-digit number, find the distance to the next ten or hundred, and prior ten or hundred.
Compose and decompose three-digit numbers into hundreds, tens and ones.
Read, write, and identify numbers up to 1000 in standard form, word form, and expanded form.
Compare two three-digit numbers using the symbols , =, based on the value of the hundreds, tens, and ones in the given numbers.
Demonstrate understanding of addition problems using properties (commutative, associative, and additive identity) within 100.
Solve addition and subtraction problems within 100, using objects, drawings, open number lines, or equations with a symbol for the unknown number in any position.
Solve addition and subtraction word problems within 100.
Add up to four two-digit numbers using multiple strategies.
Use place value understanding and visual models (e.g., base-ten blocks, number lines) to explain and justify addition and subtraction strategies up to 1000.
Given a rectangular array (up to 5 x 5), use repeated addition to find the total number of objects; write an addition equation to express the total.
Partition circles and rectangles into two, three or four equal parts then count and describe the parts using the words halves, thirds, and fourths. ("one-fourth, two-fourths, threefourths").
Explore length of an object by lining up inch-sized manipulatives with no gaps or overlaps.
Estimate the length of an object using inches, feet, and yards.
Measure the length of objects using inches, feet, and yards.
Explore length of an object by lining up centimeter and decimeter-sized manipulatives with no gaps or overlaps.
Estimate the length of an object using centimeters, decimeters, and meters.
Measure the length of objects using centimeters, decimeters, and meters.
Tell and write time to the nearest five minutes on analog and digital clocks and use a.m. and p.m. appropriately.
Solve problems involving time in 5-minute intervals.
Find the value of combinations of U.S. coins up to $1 and bills up to $100.
Identify and count coins and bills and apply that understanding to solve word problems.
Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using dollar sign and cent sign symbols appropriately.
Create tables, line plots, and bar graphs to represent a given set of data with up to four categories.
Interpret and analyze data presented with tables, line plots, picture graphs, and bar graphs.
Recognize, identify, and describe attributes (such as number of angles and number of sides) of polygons including triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and octagons.
Describe the differences between quadrilaterals (including squares, rectangles, and trapezoids) using attributes (such as congruent sides, parallel sides, and right angles).
Identify regular and irregular two-dimensional shapes.
Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.
Fluently add within 100 using various strategies.
Fluently subtract within 100 using various strategies.
Recall from memory addition facts within 20
Recall from memory subtraction facts within 20.
Mentally calculate 10 more, 10 less, 100 more and 100 less than a given three-digit number 100-900.

sets.subject: Mathematics (2026-)
sets.title: 1st Grade
sets.doc: South Dakota Mathematic Standards
standards: Count forward and backward from any number within 120.
Read, write, and identify numbers from 0 to 120.
Compose and decompose two-digit numbers into tens and ones.
Represent two-digit numbers (drawings, ten-frames, connecting cubes, base-ten blocks, place value chart, etc.).
Count objects up to 120 using groups of tens and ones.
Compare two two-digit numbers using the symbols , =, based on the value of the 10s and 1s in the given numbers.
Understand counting on as addition and counting back as subtraction.
Demonstrate understanding of addition problems using properties (commutative, associative, and additive identity) within 20.
Solve addition and subtraction problems within 20, using objects, drawings, number line, or equations with a symbol for the unknown number.
Solve addition and subtraction word problems within 20, including problems with 3 whole addends.
Given a number within 100, add and subtract multiples of 10 within 100 using multiple strategies that reflect an understanding of place value.
Add a two-digit and one-digit number (with or without regrouping) using multiple strategies that reflect an understanding of place value.
Subtract a two digit and one digit number (with or without borrowing) using multiple strategies that reflect an understanding of place value.
Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences).
Demonstrate understanding of inverse operations between addition and subtraction by creating equivalent equations within 20.
Apply the understanding of the equal sign to determine if equations involving addition or subtraction are true or false.
Given an addition or subtraction equation, find an unknown value in any position.
Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.
Measure the length of an object by lining up same-size units with no gaps or overlaps and counting the number of units.
Tell and write time to half-hour and hour intervals on analog and digital clocks.
Identify coins by name and value, including penny, nickel, dime, and quarter.
Find the value of combinations of U.S. coins up to one dollar using pennies, nickels and dimes and represent with ¢.
Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories.
Interpret and compare data represented in a picture/bar graph or tally chart.
Distinguish between defining attributes (such as triangles are three-sided) and non-defining attributes (such as color, orientation, or size).
Use defining attributes to build and draw shapes.
Compose and identify two-dimensional shapes including triangles, squares, rectangles, trapezoids, circles, half-circles, and quarter-circles.
Identify right rectangular prisms (three-dimensional solids with rectangular faces).
Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal parts and describe the parts using the words halves, fourths, and quarters and understand that more equal shares create small shares.
Recall from memory addition facts within 10.
Recall from memory subtraction facts within 10.
Mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a given two-digit number.

sets.subject: Mathematics (2026-)
sets.title: Kindergarten
sets.doc: South Dakota Mathematic Standards
standards: Count to 100 by ones and tens.
Start counting forward from any number up to 100 and count backward from any number within 20.
Read, write, and identify numbers from 0 to 20.
Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted regardless of arrangement or the order in which they were counted (cardinality).
Given a number within 20, identify one more.
Count up to 20 objects in a line, rectangular array, and circle.
Count up to 10 objects in a scattered arrangement.
For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number.
Given a number(s) from 0-20, count out that many objects.
Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the objects of another group (up to ten).
Identify whether a written number is greater than, less than, or equal to another written number (0-10).
Describe the relative positions of objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.
Represent addition and subtraction within ten using objects, fingers, drawings, mental images, or verbal explanations.
Represent the operations of addition and subtraction using an equation.
Demonstrate understanding that addition is putting together, getting more, or counting on.
Demonstrate understanding that subtraction is taking away, taking apart, or counting back.
Solve word problems, identify the correct operation needed (add or subtract within ten) and solve using objects or drawings.
Find different ways that a whole number (1 to 10) can be decomposed into two parts by using a visual representation or equation.
Find all the ways the number 5 can be broken into two parts using visual representations or equations.
Decompose and compose numbers 11-19 into tens and ones, using objects, drawings, or equations.
Describe measurable traits of an object such as length, weight, or size.
Compare objects using the same measurable trait.
Identify a clock as a tool that measures time of day. Answer questions about time of day and duration of time using both analog and digital clocks (morning, afternoon, evening, minute, hour).
Identify a calendar as a tool that measures time in days, months, weeks, years. Answer questions about time sequencing (yesterday, today, tomorrow).
Identify pennies and dimes by name and value.
Count groups of pennies and groups of dimes by their values (coins not combined).
Collect and sort objects into categories.
Identify and sort shapes as two-dimensional or three-dimensional.
Name and describe two-dimensional shapes (circles, triangles, squares, and rectangles) using attributes (sides, vertices, square corners).
Identify and draw two-dimensional shapes (circles, triangles, squares, rectangles, and trapezoid) in a variety of orientations.
Identify three-dimensional shapes (cube, cone, cylinder, or sphere).
Build and draw shapes found in the real-world.
Build simple shapes to form larger shapes.
Recognize objects within 5 (tallies, five frame, fingers, dominoes, dice, and scattered).

sets.subject: Mathematics (2026-)
sets.title: 6th Grade
sets.doc: South Dakota Mathematic Standards
standards: Understand a ratio as a comparison of two quantities.
Classify numbers (integers, fractions, decimals) as rational numbers.
Explain positive and negative integers as being opposite (inverse) values or directions from zero. Also, explain zero as its own opposite.
Understand the meaning of zero in a real-world context.
Understand the absolute value of rational numbers to be its distance from zero on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation.

Determine the absolute value of a rational number by finding its distance from zero on a number line in real-world situations; recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself.
Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.
Use visual models (e.g., area models, number lines) to explore and explain why dividing by a fraction is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal.
Use visual models (e.g., area models, number lines) to explain, justify, and apply the process of dividing fractions by fractions in real-world contexts.
Solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions.
Compare rational numbers, using inequalities (, ≤, ≥, ≠) and order on a number line.
Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100.
Find the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12.
Use the distributive property to rewrite the sum of two whole numbers 1-100 using its greatest common factor.
Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using various strategies, including but not limited to the standard algorithm.
Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals and fractions using various strategies, including but not limited to the standard algorithm.
Write ratios, rates, and unit rates. Determine the units of a unit rate.
Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems including making ratio tables, solving unit rate problems, and using percentages.
Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed.
Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100.
Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents, including those with parentheses.
Translate verbal descriptions into algebraic expressions and evaluate them for given values.
Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient, variable, constant) and view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity.

Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables, including expressions with whole number exponents and those from formulas in real-world problems. Explain how the structure of an expression affects its value by justifying each step using the order of operations and properties of operations.
Apply properties of operations (distributive, commutative, associative) to generate equivalent expressions.
Use substitution to determine if a given value in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true. Include the following inequality symbols: , ≤, ≥, ≠.
Write and solve one-step equations in real-world and mathematical problems, involving positive rational numbers and zero.
Write, solve, and graph one-step inequalities in real-world and mathematical problems, involving positive rational numbers and zero.

Understand an equation with two variables as a statement expressing a relationship between two quantities, and recognize that this relationship can often be represented as a function, where one variable depends on the other.
Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables in an equation using tables and graphs, relating these to the equation.
Find the area of triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing or decomposing to solve real-world problems.
Find the volume of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths by packing and relate it to multiplication.
Draw polygons in the coordinate plane when given coordinates for the vertices.
Use coordinates to calculate vertical and horizontal distances between points with the same 𝑥𝑥-coordinate or the same 𝑦𝑦-coordinate to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
Construct nets of a rectangular prism, rectangular pyramid, triangular prism, and triangular pyramid, using the nets to find the surface area of these prisms and pyramids.
Find and graph pairs of rational numbers in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane in realworld and mathematical problems.
Understand that signs of a coordinate pair indicate locations in a quadrant of the coordinate plane, opposite signs indicate reflections across one or both axes.
Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units within the U.S. Customary and metric measuring systems.
Understand the four components of the statistical process (question formulation, data collection, data analysis, interpretation).
Recognize that data sets collected to answer a statistical question can be analyzed by their distributions.
Represent numerical data on a number line, histogram, and box plot.
Interpret a box plot to answer statistical questions about a data set.
Distinguish between a measure of center (mean, medium, and mode) and measure of variation (range and/or mean absolute deviation).
Calculate and interpret any measure of center (mean, median, and mode) of a numerical data set.
Determine which measure of center (mean or median) is more appropriate to describe the center of data; justify the choice.
Compare and interpret range and interquartile range (IQR) to describe how data varies in a distribution.
Calculate and interpret the measure of variation (range, interquartile range (IQR), and/or mean absolute deviation) of a numerical data set.

sets.subject: Mathematics (2026-)
sets.title: 7th Grade
sets.doc: South Dakota Mathematic Standards
standards: Model and describe additive inverse in real-world situations to show opposite quantities combine to make zero (positive or negative).
Demonstrate in real-world contexts the distance between two rational numbers on the number line as the absolute value of their differences.
Convert a rational number in fraction form to decimal form and recognize that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in zeros or eventually repeats (using bar notation).
Understand that integers can be divided, provided the divisor is not zero.
Add and subtract rational numbers using horizontal or vertical number lines and real-world contexts.
Solve multi-step problems with rational numbers (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals) and justify the steps taken.
Multiply and divide rational numbers (integers, fractions, decimals etc.) in real-world and mathematical problems.
Calculate unit rates in real-world contexts that include complex fractions.
Determine the unit rate (constant of proportionality 𝑦𝑦 = 𝑘𝑘𝑘𝑘) from tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, or verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.
Solve multi-step ratio and percent problems using proportional reasoning.

Determine whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, by determining if each have a constant rate of change that starts at (0,0), using tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions.
Explain what a point (𝑥𝑥, 𝑦𝑦) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0,0) and (1, 𝑟𝑟) where 𝑟𝑟 is the unit rate.
Write and solve equations (𝑦𝑦 = 𝑘𝑘𝑘𝑘 or 𝑦𝑦 = 𝑚𝑚𝑚𝑚 + 𝑏𝑏) to represent relationships between quantities.
Add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients using multiple grouping symbols.
Write and solve two-step equations in real-world and mathematical problems in the form of 𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 + 𝑞𝑞 = 𝑟𝑟 and 𝑝𝑝(𝑥𝑥 + 𝑞𝑞) = 𝑟𝑟 where 𝑝𝑝, 𝑞𝑞, and 𝑟𝑟 are specific rational numbers.

Write, solve, and graph two-step inequalities in real-world and mathematical problems in the forms of 𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 + 𝑞𝑞 > 𝑟𝑟, 𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 + 𝑞𝑞 ≥ 𝑟𝑟, 𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 + 𝑞𝑞 < 𝑟𝑟, and 𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 + 𝑞𝑞 ≤ 𝑟𝑟, where 𝑝𝑝, 𝑞𝑞, and 𝑟𝑟 are specific rational numbers.
Use tables, graphs, and equations to distinguish between proportional and non-proportional relationships.
Identify, describe, and draw elements of circles, including center, radius, and diameter.
Use the constant ratio pi (𝜋𝜋 = 𝐶𝐶 𝑑𝑑 ) to calculate the circumference and area of a circle.
Use area (𝐴𝐴 = 𝜋𝜋𝑟𝑟2) and circumference (𝐶𝐶 = 2𝜋𝜋𝜋𝜋) formulas of a circle to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, volume and surface area of two and three-dimensional figures, as in plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids.
Describe the two-dimensional figure (cross section) that results from slicing a three-dimensional figure including right rectangular prisms, triangular prisms, pyramids and cylinders.

Draw geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
Solve multi-step problems involving supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles to include solving for an unknown angle in a figure.
Calculate the scale factor, compute the actual lengths from the scale in a drawing, and reproduce a scale drawing using another scale.
Understand sampling to be a selection of a smaller group (sample) from a larger group (population).
Compare random and convenience sampling to determine if a sample is representative of a population.
Draw conclusions, such as mean, median, mode, and range of data, about a larger population using data from a representative sample.
Understand a sample space to be the set of all possible outcomes for a situation or experiment.
Understand probability as the likelihood or chance of an event occurring.
Recognize that probabilities in a simple experiment can be qualitative descriptors of likelihood: impossible (0), unlikely, neither likely nor unlikely, likely, or certain (1).
Calculate the probability for a single event by dividing the number of favorable outcomes by the number of total outcomes.
Determine experimental probabilities in simple experiments and represent as fractions, decimals, and percents.
Use theoretical probability of an event in a simple experiment to predict the number of times that an event will occur for a large number of experiments.
Calculate the probability for a compound event using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and a simulation.

sets.subject: Mathematics (2026-)
sets.title: 5th Grade
sets.doc: South Dakota Mathematic Standards
standards: Recognize that a digit in a given place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 what it represents in the place to its left.
Use place value reasoning and patterns to explain how multiplying or dividing by powers of 10 affects the value and placement of digits in a number.
Read and write decimal numbers to the thousandths place using standard form, word form and expanded form.
Order and compare decimal numbers to the thousandths place using the symbols , =
Apply place value understanding to round decimals to any decimal place up to the hundredths place.
Write and evaluate numerical expressions with parentheses using the order of operations.
Generate two number patterns by following two different rules and make a graph using ordered pairs that match the numbers from each pattern.

Calculate whole number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors. Explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, illustrations, area models, or other representations based on place value.
Add decimals to the hundredths place using various strategies.
Subtract decimals to the hundredths place using various strategies.
Multiply decimals to the hundredths place using various strategies.
Divide decimals to the hundredths place using various strategies.
Add and subtract fractions, fractions with unlike denominators, mixed numbers, and improper fractions by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions.
Solve word problems using addition and subtraction of fractions, fractions with unlike denominators, mixed numbers, and improper fractions by using visual fraction models or equations.
Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers.
Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction. Interpret the product using visual fraction models and story contexts (e.g., area models for rectangles with fractional side lengths).

Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, including interpreting multiplication as scaling (resizing). Explain why multiplying by a fraction greater than 1 increases the product and multiplying by a fraction less than 1 decreases the product.

Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem
Interpret division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number and compute such quotients.
Interpret division of a whole number by a unit fraction and compute such quotients.
Divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions. Use visual fraction models and equations to represent and explain the relationship between multiplication and division.
Solve real-world problems involving the division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions, using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
Convert length, weight, mass, capacity, and time measurements from larger to smaller units and vice versa within the U.S. customary and metric measuring systems.
Create and use a line plot to display a data set of measurements to solve real-world problems involving information presented.
Use unit cubes and visual models to explore and explain volume as the amount of space inside a three-dimensional object.
Understand a shape has a volume of 𝑛𝑛 cubic units if it can be filled with 𝑛𝑛 unit cubes without gaps or overlaps.
Measure volume by cubic units using cubic cm, cubic in, cubic ft or cubic units.
Find the volume of right rectangular prism by packing with unit cubes and show that the volume is the same as multiplying the edge lengths (or multiplying the height by the area of the base).
Use threefold whole-number products of volume to represent the associative property of multiplication.
Solve real-world problems by applying formulas (V=l • w • h, V=B • h) for rectangular prisms to find the volume of right rectangular prisms with whole number side lengths.
Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms (with whole number side lengths) by adding the volumes.
Understand attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category.
Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.

Identify and draw triangles based on their attributes (side lengths and angle measures). Understand that triangles can be classified into categories (such as equilateral, isosceles, scalene, acute, right, and obtuse), and that these categories can overlap.
Understand a coordinate plane to be a diagram for graphing two related pieces of information with two perpendicular number lines.
Identify the origin, 𝑥𝑥-axis, and 𝑦𝑦-axis on the coordinate plane.
Identify 𝑥𝑥- and 𝑦𝑦-coordinates of points on a coordinate plane.

Understand the 𝑥𝑥-coordinate of an ordered pair as the point's location on the coordinate plane relative to the 𝑦𝑦-axis, and the 𝑦𝑦-coordinate of an ordered pair as the point's location on the coordinate plane relative to the 𝑥𝑥-axis.
Represent and interpret real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant on a coordinate plane.
Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using an algorithm, including but not limited to the standard algorithm.
Fluently divide multi-digit whole numbers using an algorithm, including but not limited to the standard algorithm.

sets.subject: Mathematics (2026-)
sets.title: 4th Grade
sets.doc: South Dakota Mathematic Standards
standards: Recognize that a digit in a given place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.
Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
Compose and decompose five-digit numbers into ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones.
Read and write whole numbers up to 1,000,000 using standard form, word form, and expanded form.
Compare two multi-digit numbers based on values of the digits in each place value using the symbols , =.
Represent and explain multiplicative comparisons using equations, drawings, and verbal reasoning.

Solve real-world problems involving multiplicative comparison, using drawings and/or equations with a symbol for the unknown number, and distinguish between multiplicative comparison and additive comparison.
Multiply four-digit whole numbers by one-digit whole numbers, and multiply two two-digit whole numbers.
Divide four digit whole numbers by one-digit divisors; quotients should be with and without whole number remainders.
Interpret a remainder of a one-step division problem.

Solve multistep word problems using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, with whole numbers and having whole number answers, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted; assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
Find factor pairs for whole numbers up to 100.
Recognize that a whole number (within 100) is a multiple of each of its factors.
Find multiples of single-digit whole numbers.
Determine whether a whole number from 1 to 100 is prime or composite.
Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule, identifying apparent features of the pattern that are not explicit in the rule itself.
Demonstrate understanding of addition and multiplication problems using properties (commutative, associative, distributive, and identity).
Evaluate a numerical expression including addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division using the order of operations of whole numbers without parenthesis and exponents.
Use visual models and reasoning to explain why a fraction 𝑎𝑎/𝑏𝑏 is equivalent to another fraction when both the numerator and denominator are multiplied by the same number.
Compare fractions with different numerators and denominators, by creating common denominators or numerators, using the symbols , =.
Add and subtract fractions with like denominators.
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators.
Break apart fractions into sums of fractions with the same denominator and smaller numerators.
Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators using various strategies.
Multiply a fraction by a whole number and a whole number by a fraction.
Understand a fraction 𝑎𝑎/𝑏𝑏 is a multiple of 1/𝑏𝑏.
Understand a multiple of 𝑎𝑎/𝑏𝑏 is also a multiple of 1/𝑏𝑏.
Solve word problems involving multiplication of fractions by whole numbers.
Add two fractions with denominator of 10 and 100 by expressing the denominator of 10 as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of 100.
Understand a decimal number to be a number with a whole part and a fractional part separated by a decimal point.
Apply decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100; locate these decimals on a number line.
Read, write, and describe the value of decimal numbers to the hundredths place.
Compare decimals to the hundredths place on a number line and by using the symbols , =.
Measure length, weight, mass, and capacity using U.S. Customary and metric systems of measurement (including km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz.; l, ml; hr, min, sec.).
Express larger units in terms of smaller units through conversions within a single system of measurement.
Solve word problems using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division involving distance, intervals of time, capacity, masses, and money, using fractional and decimal values.
Use visual models and reasoning to explain how area and perimeter formulas for rectangles relate to their side lengths and solve real-world problems.
Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and solve problems using the line plot.
Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed where two rays share a common endpoint.
Measure angles in degrees using a protractor and understand a degree as 1/360 of a circle; draw angles of specific measure.
Classify angles as right, acute, obtuse, or straight. Draw right, acute, obtuse, and straight angles.
Recognize and apply the concept of additive angles: when angles are broken apart the sum of the parts is equal to the angle measure of the whole.
Identify, describe, and draw points, lines, segments, rays, and angles.
Identify, describe, and draw intersecting, parallel, and perpendicular lines.
Understand a trapezoid to be a two-dimensional shape with four sides, where exactly one pair of sides is parallel.
Identify and describe various quadrilaterals by their properties of parallel and perpendicular lines including square, rectangle, trapezoid, and rhombus.
Identify, describe, and draw equilateral, scalene, right, acute, and obtuse angles and triangles.
Identify and draw lines of symmetry for two-dimensional figures.
Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using an algorithm including, but not limited to, the standard algorithm.
